nameStory: The southern flounder gets its name from being the most common flounder species in the southeastern United States, ranging from the Carolinas down through the Gulf of Mexico. While it occasionally ventures north into New England waters, it's definitely a warm-water fish that prefers the balmy southern coastlines where it thrives year-round.
description: The southern flounder is a large, flat fish that lives on the ocean bottom with both eyes on its left side - making it a 'left-eyed flounder.' Like all flounders, it starts life swimming upright like a normal fish, but as it grows, one eye migrates over to join the other, and the fish settles onto the seafloor on its right side. It's the biggest flounder in the western Atlantic, capable of reaching impressive sizes that make it a prized catch for both sport and commercial fishermen. Its flattened body is perfectly designed for life on sandy and muddy bottoms where it ambushes prey.

idTips.label: Body Shape
idTips.description: Extremely flattened, diamond-shaped body that feels firm and muscular when handled, with the pigmented left side facing up and pale right side facing down

idTips.label: Eye Position
idTips.description: Both eyes located on the left side of the head - if you're looking at the fish head-on and see both eyes, you're looking at the left side

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Brown to olive-green on the pigmented side with darker spots and mottling that can change to match the bottom, while the underside is stark white

idTips.label: Mouth
idTips.description: Large mouth with sharp teeth that extends past the lower eye, designed for grabbing fish and crabs - handle with care as those teeth can puncture skin

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: The largest flounder species in our region, with adults commonly exceeding the size of a dinner plate and feeling surprisingly heavy for a flatfish

habitat: In New England, southern flounders are extremely rare visitors found only occasionally in the warmest coastal waters, typically around sandy or muddy bottoms in shallow bays and estuaries. They prefer areas with soft sediments where they can bury themselves, usually in waters less than 30 feet deep. When present, they're most likely found in the southernmost parts of our region during the warmest months.

seasonality.spring: Extremely rare in New England waters, but any sightings would most likely begin in late spring as waters warm.
seasonality.summer: Peak time for any potential sightings in our region's warmest coastal waters and protected bays.
seasonality.fall: May linger into early fall in unusually warm years, but typically absent from New England by this time.
seasonality.winter: Completely absent from New England waters, having moved south to warmer regions.

funFact: Southern flounders are masters of disguise that can actually change their skin color and pattern in just seconds to perfectly match the seafloor beneath them - they do this so well that they can even attempt to mimic a checkerboard pattern when placed on one in laboratory experiments!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with the much more common summer flounder, but southern flounders are generally larger, have a bigger mouth that extends past the lower eye, and lack the distinct eye-spots that summer flounders often display. Remember: if you're in New England and find a large left-eyed flounder, it's almost certainly a summer flounder unless you're having an extremely rare encounter.
contextualKnowledge: Despite being called 'southern' flounder, this species occasionally shows up in unexpected places during warm water years, leading to exciting rare fish reports. The single observation recorded in New England represents the northern edge of this species' range and highlights how ocean warming can bring southern species into new territories.
compareHints: Compared to its close relative the summer flounder, southern flounders are typically larger with a proportionally bigger mouth and less distinct spotting patterns. Unlike the fourspot flounder which has four distinctive eye-spots, southern flounders have more irregular mottled patterns. Summer flounders are much more common in New England and have a mouth that doesn't extend as far past the eye.

relatedSpecies.distinction: Summer flounder are larger and more robust than their cousin the fourspot flounder, which has four distinctive dark spots and rarely exceeds 12 inches.
Compared to its close relative the Summer Flounder, the Fourspot Flounder has more distinct, evenly-spaced spots rather than irregular blotches and mottling.
